content:
The unemployment rate doesn’t count everyone who doesn’t have a job.

Its denominator is the number of employed people plus the number classified as unemployed. That classification depends on what happened during specific survey periods.

In general, a person must not have been employed during the reference week, must have been available for work (with an exception for temporary illness), and must have actively looked for work during the four weeks ending with that week.

There’s an exception to the active-search requirement: someone on temporary layoff who expects to be recalled may qualify without searching. By contrast, browsing job listings alone doesn’t count as actively looking.

So having no job isn’t enough by itself. Availability, recent job-search activity, and the temporary-layoff exception determine whether someone is counted as unemployed—and included in the rate’s denominator.
